observations.content:
Summary: Python was first released by Guido van Rossum in February 1991 as Python 0.9.0. This initial release included core features such as exception handling, functions, and core data types like list, dict, and str. The first public release was made on February 20, 1991, and it was released to alt.sources newsgroup. The language had been in development since December 1989, and internal versions existed before 0.9.0, but 0.9.0 was the first version made publicly available outside CWI.

args.query: Rust 1.0 released year May 2015 Rust 1.0 stable release date

observations.content:
Summary: The first stable release of Rust, Rust 1.0, was published on May 15, 2015, according to the sources. This release marked a significant change in Rust development, committing to backwards compatibility and stability. The sources confirm that May 15, 2015, was the release date of Rust 1.0, making May 15, 2025, the 10-year anniversary of this release.

[1] Rust (programming language) - Wikipedia
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_(programming_language)
    On May 15, 2015, Rust 1.0 became the first stable release. One year later, the compiler had accumulated at least 1,400 contributors, and there were at least 5,000 third-party libraries published on the package management website Crates.io.: 43:15

### 2015–2020: Servo and early adoption

[edit&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2015–2020: Servo and early adoption")] [...] Software developer Graydon Hoare created Rust in 2006 while working at Mozilla, which officially sponsored the project in 2009. The first stable release, Rust 1.0, was published in May 2015. The project has been sponsored by the Rust Foundation since February 2021. It has been adopted by many software projects, especially web services and system software. It has been studied academically and has a growing community of developers.

## History [...] Work shifted from the OCaml compiler to a self-hosting compiler (i.e., written in Rust) targeting LLVM. The ownership system was in place by 2010. The Rust logo was developed in 2011 based on a bicycle chainring. The early 2010s witnessed increasing involvement from full-time engineers at Mozilla and open source contributors.

On January 20, 2012, Rust 0.1 became the first public release for Windows, Linux, and MacOS.

### 2012–2015: Evolution

[2] Rust: A systems programming language | by Mario García | Medium
    https://medium.com/@mattdark/rust-a-systems-programming-language-272ca761dfa0
    ## About

Rust is a systems programming language developed by the engineers of Mozilla. Rust could be categorized as a new language, as Rust 1.0, the first stable version was released on May 15th, 2015. The latest version today is Rust 1.20, that was released on August 31st, this year.

Rust is a compiled language like C or C++.

[3] Rust 2015 - The Rust Edition Guide
    https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2015/index.html
    # Rust 2015

Rust 2015 has a theme of “stability”. It commenced with the release of 1.0, and is the “default edition”. The edition system was conceived in late 2017, but Rust 1.0 was released in May of 2015. As such, 2015 is the edition that you get when you don’t specify any particular edition, for backwards compatibility reasons. [...] “Stability” is the theme of Rust 2015 because 1.0 marked a huge change in Rust development. Previous to Rust 1.0, Rust was changing on a daily basis. This made it very difficult to write large software in Rust, and made it difficult to learn. With the release of Rust 1.0 and Rust 2015, we committed to backwards compatibility, ensuring a solid foundation for people to build projects on top of. [...] Since it’s the default edition, there’s no way to port your code to Rust 2015; it just is. You’ll be transitioning away from 2015, but never really to 2015. As such, there’s not much else to say about it!

[4] 1.0.0 | Rust Changelogs
    https://releases.rs/docs/1.0.0
    ### 1.0.0

# 1.0.0 #

>  Released on: 15 May, 2015
>  Branched from master on: 4 December, 2015

 ~1500 changes, numerous bugfixes

## Highlights #

 The vast majority of the standard library is now `#[stable]`. It is no longer possible to use unstable features with a stable build of the compiler.
 Many popular crates on crates.io now work on the stable release channel.
 Arithmetic on basic integer types now checks for overflow in debug builds.

## Language # [...] The path API was revised to normalize `.`, adjusting the tradeoffs in favor of the most common usage.
 A large number of remaining APIs in `std` were also stabilized

I know Rust had earlier versions and pre-1.0 milestones, but I’m specifically referring to the 1.0 stable release. Can anyone confirm if May 15, 2015 was the correct release date, and if so, does that make May 15, 2025 the actual 10-year anniversary instead of May 8?

Would really appreciate any cla

answer: Python was first released in **1991** [S1], and that was **24 years before** Rust’s 1.0 release in **2015** [S6][S9].
